safavid-empire.summary: Established Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion of Iran and contested Mesopotamia and the Caucasus with the Ottomans for two centuries.

transatlantic-slave-trade.summary: Over three and a half centuries, more than twelve million Africans were shipped to the Americas to be worked, overwhelmingly on sugar, cotton and tobacco plantations. It was the largest forced migration in history and the foundation of the plantation economies of the Atlantic world.
transatlantic-slave-trade.significance: The plantation economies it built financed much of European industrialisation. It is not a side story to the modern world's formation; it is load-bearing.
transatlantic-slave-trade.note: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database records roughly 12.5 million people embarked and about 10.7 million surviving the crossing — a figure built from surviving voyage records, so a floor rather than a total.

image.credit: Plymouth Chapter of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade

reformation.summary: Western Christianity split, and with it the assumption that there was one authority over belief in Europe — a quarrel over indulgences that print turned into a continental war within a generation.
reformation.note: The end is a choice. 1555 is the Peace of Augsburg, which let German princes pick their church; 1648 is Westphalia, after the wars of religion had killed perhaps a third of the German population. The bracket holds both.

fall-of-tenochtitlan.summary: A two-year campaign ending in a siege, in which smallpox and indigenous allies mattered more than Spanish numbers. The city was razed and Mexico City built on it.

european-contact-pacific.summary: From Magellan's crossing to Cook's three voyages, European charting of the Pacific was followed within a generation by disease, missionaries and annexation.

mughal-empire.summary: Founded when Babur defeated the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat, the Mughal state came to rule most of the subcontinent, fused Persian and Indian artistic traditions, and survived in name until the British deposed Bahadur Shah II after 1857.
mughal-empire.significance: At its height it may have produced a quarter of the world's economic output. Its decline and the East India Company's rise are the same event viewed from two ends.

fall-of-the-inca.summary: Pizarro seized the emperor at Cajamarca with fewer than two hundred men, exploiting a civil war and an epidemic that had already killed the previous ruler. Resistance continued from Vilcabamba for forty years.

akbar.summary: Third Mughal emperor, who acceded at thirteen in 1556, abolished the jizya, took Rajput wives and allies, and convened debates between Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Jesuit scholars at Fatehpur Sikri.
akbar.significance: He abolished the tax on non-Muslims and staged public debates between rival faiths while Europe was fighting its wars of religion. Tulsidas was writing in Awadhi during the same reign.

cocoliztli-epidemics.summary: Two catastrophic outbreaks in New Spain, the first killing an estimated five to fifteen million people in the Mexican highlands.
cocoliztli-epidemics.note: The cause is unresolved; a 2018 study recovered Salmonella enterica DNA from victims, but indigenous viral haemorrhagic fever is still argued.

potosi-silver.summary: A single mountain produced a large share of the world's silver for two centuries, financing the Spanish empire and flowing on to China. It was worked under the mita labour draft at a cost in indigenous and African lives that contemporaries already described as devouring men.

tycho-brahe.summary: Measured the positions of the planets with unmatched precision for the naked eye, producing the data Kepler later made sense of.

cervantes.summary: Maimed at Lepanto, held five years by Algerian pirates, and author of Don Quixote, which is usually called the first modern novel because it is about someone who has read too many of the old ones.
cervantes.note: He and Shakespeare died within about ten days of each other, though not on the same day — England and Spain were using different calendars.

mughal-painting.summary: Persian technique in an Indian workshop under imperial patronage, turned towards portraits, animals and court record — and largely abandoned by the state after Aurangzeb withdrew his interest.

galileo.summary: Turned the telescope on the sky, found moons around Jupiter and phases on Venus, and was tried by the Inquisition for saying what they meant.

shakespeare.summary: Thirty-eight plays and 154 sonnets written for a commercial playhouse, which have since been translated into more languages than any other secular body of work.
shakespeare.note: Baptised 26 April 1564; the birth date of 23 April is a convention.

bijak-kabir.summary: Kabir was probably illiterate and certainly did not write a book; what survives was collected by followers from oral circulation, decades to centuries after his death.
bijak-kabir.note: Three separate traditions preserve different Kabirs — the Bijak of the Kabir Panth, the Guru Granth Sahib selection, and the Rajasthani manuscripts. They disagree on wording and on which verses are his at all.

kepler.summary: Replaced circular orbits with ellipses and found the three laws that govern planetary motion.

ramcharitmanas.summary: The counter-example in this file — an author writing his own book in his own lifetime, in the spoken Awadhi rather than Sanskrit, and so putting the story of Rama directly into the mouths of people who could not read it otherwise.

texts.title: Hindu texts at the Internet Sacred Text Archive

descartes.summary: Tried to doubt everything and found he could not doubt that he was doubting, making the thinking self the starting point of modern philosophy.
